🚀 Feature
Implement a join context for the ZeroRedundancyOptimizer (and distributed optimizers in general).
Motivation
Uneven inputs in DDP lead to a NCCL communication error due to nodes missing in the allreduce phase during gradient updates. This is resolved by running the training loop in an model.join() context, which shadows forward and backward passes by inserting communication operations where necessary. For the newly introduced ZeroRedundancyOptimizer there is no such context, therefore uneven inputs lead to NCCL crashes again. It would be great to have a similar shadowing functionality for the ZeroRedundancyOptimizer and all future distributed optimizers.
Pitch
Add a .join() context similar to DistributedDataParallel.join() to distributed optimizers, specifically ZeroRedundancyOptimizer.
Alternatives
I don't like the idea of opening two contexts for the training loop, but if the optimizer is supposed to be kept separate from the model, I don't see a way to put them into the same context.
Additional context
I ran into this issue while training a DDP model on uneven inputs. Since training fails with the ZeroRedundancyOptimizer and DDP but not with regular optimizers, I strongly suspect what I described here is what's happening. There might be something I've missed, but given that my errors look exactly the same as running DDP without the join() context and the behaviour is to be expected, I'm fairly confident this is the issue.

🐛 Bug
As per title. See the code example below.
To Reproduce
>>> import torch                                                                                                                                                      [7/182]
>>> b = torch.rand(3, 3, dtype=torch.cdouble)                                                                                                                                
>>> a = torch.rand(3, 3, dtype=torch.cdouble).triu()                                                                                                                         
>>> at = a.transpose(-1, -2)                                                                                                                                                 
>>> (a @ x - b).abs().max()
tensor(1.2413e-16, dtype=torch.float64)
>>> y = torch.triangular_solve(b, at, upper=False).solution
>>> (at @ y - b).abs().max()
tensor(1.3878e-16, dtype=torch.float64)
>>> z = torch.triangular_solve(b, at, transpose=True).solution
>>> (a @ z - b).abs().max()
tensor(1.8858, dtype=torch.float64)
>>> z = torch.triangular_solve(b, at, transpose=True, upper=False).solution
>>> (a @ z - b).abs().max()
tensor(1.2413e-16, dtype=torch.float64)
The documentation says that transpose controls whether the input is to be transposed before the driver is applied.
Also, upper is explained as a parameter that decides whether to solve an upper/lower triangular system.
What is the connection between upper and triangular? Are they independent or not?
Apparently, upper=True actually means that the input (prior to transposition) is upper triangular, and is lower triangular when upper=False,
which you can indeed infer from the fact that upper precedes transpose in the list of arguments, but it is still could be confusing given how upper is defined.
The relationship between upper and transpose has to be clarified in greater details.

Possible choices of default_rtol:

NumPy uses eps * max(rows, cols) for matrix_rank and 1e-15 for pinv
TensorFlow uses the same default as NumPy for matrix_rank but 10 * eps * max(rows, cols) for pinv
JAX uses the same defaults as TensorFlow
Julia uses eps * min(rows, cols) both for pinv and matrix_rank

Use of max(atol, rtol * ...) for defining the truncation criteria follows math.isclose.
Backwards compatibility / NumPy compatibility:
def matrix_rank(input, tol = None):
    if tol is None:
        return matrix_rank(input, atol = 0, rtol = eps * max(rows, cols))
    else:
        return matrix_rank(input, atol = tol, rtol = 0)

def pinv(input, rcond = 1e-15)

🚀 Feature
Implement GPU/CPU kernels for efficient regularized Wasserstein distance computation (Sinkhorn).
Motivation
The regularized Wasserstein distance between samples is a frequent metric used in various deep learning models.
One intuitive way to think about it is that it is a distance (in the underlying space)-aware alternative to KL divergence for measuring distances between probability measures.
In the time since Cuturi from 2013 and Frogner et al. from 2015, this has developed into a very useful general purpose tool. Recent notable applications using the Wasserstein distance include SwAV, but it is also of interest more generally to compare probability distributions or interpolate between them.
One key computational challenge is that stable implementation requires (more or less) a matrix multiplication using logsumexp instead of regular dot products, this is much easier to get with a custom kernel. (And logsumexp is much more stable than factoring out large scalars which has been proposed as a make-do stabilization.)
Pitch
I propose to implement a sinkhorn kernel.
Alternatives
Implement it a specialized library, but I think the applications are numerous and general enough to warrant inclusion into PyTorch proper.
Additional context
Related: #51777

        x = F.relu(self.fc2(x))

def train(gpu, args):
    
    rank = args['nr'] * args['gpus'] + gpu                          
    dist.init_process_group(                                   
        backend='nccl',                                         
        init_method='env://',                                   
        world_size=args['world_size'],                              
        rank=rank                                               
    )
    
    torch.cuda.set_device(gpu)
    
    ## Dataset
    transform = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.ToTensor(),
    transforms.Normalize((0.5, 0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5, 0.5))
    ])

    train_data = datasets.CIFAR10('CIFAR10_data/', train=True, download=True, transform=transform)
    valid_data = datasets.CIFAR10('CIFAR10_data/', train=False, download=True, transform=transform)
    
    train_sampler = torch.utils.data.distributed.DistributedSampler(
    	train_data,
    	num_replicas=args['world_size'],
    	rank=rank,
    )
    
    batch_size = len(train_data)//args['world_size']
    
    if gpu == 0:
        print(batch_size)

    train_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(train_data, batch_size=batch_size, sampler=train_sampler)
    valid_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(valid_data, batch_size=batch_size)
    
    ##Model
    
    model = img_classifier().cuda(gpu)
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    optimizer = optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.02)
    
    model = nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel(model, device_ids=[gpu])
    
    n_epochs = 20
    valid_loss_min = np.Inf

    for epoch in range(1, n_epochs+1):

        train_loss = 0.0
        valid_loss = 0.0

        model.train()
               
        for data, target in train_loader:
            if torch.cuda.is_available:
                data, target = data.cuda(), target.cuda()
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            output = model(data)
            loss = criterion(output, target)
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()
            train_loss += loss.item()*data.size(0)


        # validate the model
        if gpu==0 :
            model.eval()
            for data, target in valid_loader:
                if torch.cuda.is_available:
                    data, target = data.cuda(), target.cuda()
                output = model(data)
                loss = criterion(output, target)
                valid_loss += loss.item()*data.size(0)

            # calculate average losses
            train_loss = train_loss/len(train_loader.dataset)
            valid_loss = valid_loss/len(valid_loader.dataset)

            # print training/validation statistics 
            print('Epoch: {} \tTraining Loss: {:.6f} \tValidation Loss: {:.6f}'.format(
                epoch, train_loss, valid_loss))

            # save model if validation loss has decreased
            if valid_loss <= valid_loss_min:
                print('Validation loss decreased ({:.6f} --> {:.6f}).  Saving model ...'.format(
                valid_loss_min,
                valid_loss))
                torch.save(model.state_dict(), 'model_cifar.pt')
                valid_loss_min = valid_loss

        dist.barrier()
        
def main():
    args = {
        'gpus' : 2,
        'nodes' : 1,
        'nr': 0
    }
    
    args['world_size'] = args['gpus'] * args['nodes']
    mp.spawn(train, nprocs=args['gpus'], args=(args,))
    
    
if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
Expected behavior

After #52964, I failed to build PyTorch on Windows due to the lacking of intel-openmp. I did my investigation and found the following things:

conda install intel-openmp: installs the libiomp5md.dll and related, but NOT headers.
conda install mkl mkl-include: installs the MKL libraries & headers, but NOT anything OpenMP.
This link used in #52964: include both libraries & headers for both MKL & OpenMP.

So how do we expect users to build the code right now, using intel-openmp? The current instruction no longer works.

nodes.bodyText:
see #53742 for discussion.

When using CUDA RPC, if the user function uses a new device which is not used by any Tensors in the request, current TensorPipeAgent cannot properly synchronize communication and computation. This is because the agent cannot predict which devices a user function will use and is not aware of which stream on that device it should wait for. Two naive solutions might be 1) create a context/stream for all available devices, 2) always synchronize with current/default stream on the new device. However, neither of these would work. The first one would create CUDA context on a device even if the device was not used in the RPC. As a result, it would introduce additional CUDA memory overhead, or worse, lead to deadlock. The second one will sync all background RPCs to the same current/default stream, which would interfere with user logic on the user main thread and contentions on that stream could lead to performance problem and correctness might be hard to argue.


Besides, we still need to solve the problem of CPU-request + CUDA-response, where we don't have an existing stream at all. One possibility might be letting users to specify streams for the user function.

Based the discussion in #53742, instead of introducing new APIs to fix the problem, we are going to disallow using new devices in output for now and also disable corresponding tests to avoid flakiness in master. We will add it back when we reach consensus on the API.

🚀 Feature
Provide a util function for creating per-machine process groups as subgroups of the global communication world and returning the subgroup corresponding to the current machine.
Motivation
Some communication optimizations in distributed training may require intra-node communications among the processes within each machine.
For example, since intra-node communication is usually much cheaper than inter-node communication, some parallel SGD algorithms like hierarchical averaging SGD run intra-node allreduce more frequently, and inter-node/global allreduce less frequently, rather than always use the same synchronization frequency globally.
Another example can be SyncBatchNorm. As the tutorial shows, torch.nn.SyncBatchNorm can be applied to subgroups rather than the whole communication world. Such subgroup can often be a per-machine process group in practice.
A few DL algorithms initialize their own per-machine process groups in customized communication libraries.

Detectron2
SlowFast

It would be nice for PyTorch to provide a util function to initialize per-machine process groups. Particularly, a caveat of torch.distributed.new_group API is that, even if every rank eventually will only use a single per-machine process group, it must initialize all the per-machine process groups. This can be easily neglected by the users when writing their own implementations. Particularly, #48804 updated SyncBatchNorm tutorial to emphasize this point. (I have also seen some use cases that use the less performant DataParallel instead of DistributedDataParallel to avoid the error-prone initialization of per-machine process groups.)
API
In distributed_c10d.py, we can add a util function, which initializes all the local process groups (e.g., per-machine intra-node process groups), and returns the one corresponding to the current rank.
def init_local_process_groups(local_world_size: int, process_group: torch.distributed.ProcessGroup, tiemout: datatime.timedelta, backend: str) -> torch.distributed.ProcessGroup:
where local_world_size can be the number of GPUs per machine for this case.
